title: But the word of Mr Costello was an unwelcome language for him for he nauseated the wretch that seemed to him a cropeared creature of a misshapen gibbosity, born out of wedlock and thrust like a crookback toothed and feet first into the world, which the dint of the surgeon’s pliers in his skull lent indeed a colour to, so as to put him in thought of that missing link of creation’s chain desiderated by the late ingenious Mr Darwin.
html_source:
While impersonating Burke, Joyce can’t resist an allusion to Shakespeare here. In Act V, Scene VI of Henry VI, Gloucester, who would soon become Richard III, stabs the protagonist, who has just compared himself to Daedalus, and his son to Icarus, and exclaims:

“I, that have neither pity, love, nor fear.
Indeed, ‘tis true that Henry told me of;
For I have often heard my mother say
I came into the world with my legs forward.”

Gloucester/Richard, we know, was born with a “crookback” deformity, and Joyce’s addition of “gibbosity,” which also means “hunchbacked”, further establishes the mention, whose purpose here is not only to echo “Burke’s” denouncing Irish youth as having “neither pity, love, nor fear,” but is also to point us to the Ulysses-specific reference to Daedalus and Icarus. The key to this reference occurs in the “"Scylla and Charybdis” episode as Stephen is expounding his Shakespeare/Hamlet theory. Stephen is brought to remember the final entry in his diary in A Portrait*:

“Fabulous artificer. The hawklike man. You flew. Whereto? Newhaven-Dieppe,steerage passenger. Paris and back. Lapwing. Icarus. Pater, ait. Seabedabbled, fallen, weltering.Lapwing you are. Lapwing be.”

What is the significance of “lapwing”? George L. Geckle, in his Winter 1969 article in the James Joyce Quarterly, takes us to an unsurprising third level of depth in answering it; William M. Schutte, quoting from Blake’s Gnomic Verses, describes a lapwing and then observes, “Blake’s lapwing, flying around on the barren heath instead of where the corn grows, ignorant both of where the soil is fruitful… , is a good symbol for the ambitious but often misdirected young man to whom Stephen refers… , a young man that could fly by all the nets that sought to restrain him.” Geckle argues that, while some critics may argue that Joyce would have been aware of the implications of these references, Stephen would not. He writes, “The Stephen in Ulysses, I would argue, becomes well aware of the implications of his references, especially when such references show the irony of his past aspirations and present failures. The ‘lapwing’ passage is proof that such is the case.”
